Eva Phillips (Joan Crawford) dominates her Georgia mansion and her facially-scarred husband Avery (Barry Sullivan), nicknamed "Beauty", an alcoholic mill-owner who hates her. A cousin, Jennifer Stewart (Lucy Marlow), is pressured into moving in with the family, and she watches in horror as Eva maneuvers to prevent the marriage of Avery's sister Carol (Betsy Palmer), an equestrian, to Avery's business manager Judson Prentiss (John Ireland), who had secretly been involved with Eva in the past. Jennifer learns that Eva stole Avery from house guest Sue McKinnon (Fay Wray), who has been mentally disturbed ever since.
Jennifer briefly dates Sue's suave brother Ty, but it doesn't last long. Meanwhile, as tension builds among the various denizens of the mansion, Avery shoots Eva's terminally-ill dog, telling people to lie to Eva and say the dog had died naturally. Jennifer says she doesn't like to lie, and Avery says Eva would prefer to be lied to.
Carol tells Jennifer to watch out for Eva, and that she read a book about bees and feels that Eva is like a queen bee who stings all her competitors to death. Jennifer refuses to believe such bad sentiments about Eva, and eventually becomes her putative personal assistant, and a caretaker to the young Phillips children, Tessa and Ted. Ted persistently has intense nightmares about a fatal car crash involving his parents.
That same night, Eva and Jud have a meeting in a darkened room where he tells her that their relationship and anything they had together was over because he is marrying Carol. Eva rejects this and begins to kiss him, but Judson stops kissing her after a few seconds once he realizes that he is falling back into her trap.
Meanwhile, Jennifer witnesses this rendezvous from the top of the staircase and is shocked. Jud turns the light on and tells Eva that he is serious, and she warns him that he will ultimately be sorry for refusing her. When Carol and Jud's engagement is announced to Eva, Eva strongly hints at her former affair with Jud, and Carol commits suicide by hanging herself in the horse stable.
Avery catches nanny Miss Breen acting abusively towards the children, and fires her. Meanwhile, Jennifer and Avery are drawn together and share a furtive kiss when he tells her that he is aware of Eva and Jud's past. Eva senses the developing relationship and increases her malevolent actions; she insists Miss Breen continue as nanny, and tells Avery to not interact with Jennifer any longer. When he refuses, she threatens a scandalous divorce in the press.
Meanwhile, Jud, still guilty over Carol's death, leaves the house for a few weeks, but comes back one day for work. He finds out from Jennifer that it was really Eva who told Carol about his earlier relationship with Eva, not Avery as he had assumed. Now, for different reasons, both men are determined to avenge it.
Avery, after glancing over his gun cabinet, changes his outward attitude completely, and acts as though he is in love with Eva, even giving her an expensive bracelet. She changes her attitude and says that she is done being manipulative because her husband finally loves her. However, Jud sees through the charade and confronts Avery, stating that Avery's true motive for being nice to Eva is so that she will trust him enough so that he can kill her.
Jud preempts his plan on the night Avery intends to commit murder-suicide, and drives Eva to the fancy-dress party to which Avery would have driven her. When Eva discerns that he wants her dead, she frantically attacks him, resulting in a crash over a cliff, killing them both. Before learning of his mother's death, Ted has another dream about a fatal car crash. Now, Jennifer and Avery are free to love each other.
story_text_b:
# Action and style
The novel is about the inhabitants of a city that is the site of a strange experiment of unknown nature. Andrej Woronin, a volunteer participant, lives there and seeks to spread his ideologically endowed categories of thought  the examination of which is ultimately abstracted to the question of the meaning of life. But that's hard in this place, because "the experiment is the experiment" and it's the reason for a lot of obscure things. For example, the city is overrun by baboons for no apparent reason; the sun (or what serves as the sun) is turned off in the evening and turned on again in the morning to create an artificial day/night cycle  but it can also happen that the sun remains off for 14 days; the red building appears out of nowhere every evening and disappears again in the early morning  once after a virtual game of chess. Across the country stretches a seemingly endless and therefore insurmountable yellow wall and the like.
Even more mysterious, however, is the origin of the volunteers in the experiment. These come not only from the most diverse countries but also from the most diverse periods of time. Nevertheless, normal verbal communication is possible: each one seems to speak the other's mother tongue. The main character Andrei Woronin, for example, is a Russian stellar astronomer from the 1950s, while his friend Fritz Geiger is a German Wehrmacht non-commissioned officer who came to the experiment shortly after the Second World War. Other people are from the '60s and '70s. One of the rules of the experiment is the permanent, random occupational rotation of all citizens, across social strata, from plumbers to the highest positions of power. A personal "mentor" (similar to the character "Kamillo" in "The Distant Rainbow" by A. and B. Strugazki) surprises Andrei at turning points in the story, but involuntarily usually only causes further confusion.
At the beginning of the novel, the main character Andrej is still a simple garbage driver, but after that he first becomes a criminal officer and later editor-in-chief of a newspaper. After a coup by Fritz Geiger and his followers, who deposed the mayor and the old hierarchy and became president, Andrej also rises further in the social hierarchy and becomes one of President Geiger's advisors (quasi-minister of research). Finally, a dangerous scientific expedition is launched into the unknown north, which he leads as leader. Only he and a close friend are left, torturing themselves through endless deserts, and the reader is faced with an analysis of the universe, creation, or civilization; symbolized by a tower or temple that is analogous to the great changes of culture as well as the far-reaching individual contribution of one man to architecturally variable, never finished. People portray themselves as architects or workers, priests or pilgrims. Although there have been some setbacks, the result is that this construction has proved to be indestructible. After a brief stay in an oasis, or even the Garden of Eden  mentioned only retrospectively, almost hallucinatory, the hikers voluntarily move on. In the final pages, possibly in the afterlife or a death fantasy, the mentor has the final say, and Andrej has described the first ontological circle...
'The Experiment' is an intellectual book that deals almost exclusively with Andrey's political, ideological or historical-philosophical reflections. Nevertheless, the plot moves forward, and idyllic moments develop. As you read, it quickly becomes clear that these are only hypothetical questions, ideas, or images that cannot be decided.

story_text_a: Casey, an American living in Cologne, Germany, works with his friend Matthias for a drug dealer, Geran, as money runners. He meets Juliette, another American, one night while she tends bar at one of Geran's hangouts. Though interested in him, Juliette turns him down when he asks her out, stating that she wants nothing to do with someone who runs in Geran's circles, but to look her up when he gets out. Inspired by the conversation, Casey quits his job with Geran, asks Juliette out, and the two quickly begin dating and move in together. All is well for the pair until Juliette suddenly has a seizure one evening and is rushed to the hospital. Told that her kidney is failing, and because she is not a citizen of Germany that she is unqualified for the transplant treatment, Casey proposes that they move back to America for her treatment. In order to obtain the money for the operation and save Juliette, Casey goes back to work for Geran in order to pull off a large drug theft from Germany's biggest drug dealer, Hagen Kahl.
story_text_b: Casey (Nicholas Hoult) se ha enamorado de Juliette (Felicity Jones). Cuando a Juliette le diagnostican una enfermedad mortal, Casey elabora un plan para robarle a Hagen (Anthony Hopkins), un peligroso criminal, y poder pagar el tratamiento médico que salvaría la vida de Juliette. El plan de Casey, sin embargo, no sale como él espera. Tendrá que emprender una huida en coche por toda Alemania para salvar su vida y llegar a Juliette antes de que los hombres de Hagen la encuentren primero.

story_text_a:
La historia mezcla detalles de la vida contemporánea con un bárbaro ritual llamado "la lotería". La historia ocurre en una pequeña ciudad estadounidense (de aproximadamente 300 habitantes) donde los moradores muestran un humor extraño y sombrío, y donde se observan cosas no usuales, como niños que cogen y reúnen piedras para la lotería anual del 27 de junio.
El sorteo se realiza entre los cabezas de familia, y son elegidos los Hutchinson. Después, se realiza un sorteo dentro de la familia elegida, y sale escogida Tessie Hutchinson (la madre), por lo que es lapidada hasta la muerte por todos los vecinos del pueblo, incluida su propia familia, como un sacrificio necesario para asegurar una buena cosecha, conforme a las creencias de la comunidad.
story_text_b:
In an unnamed American village, at first allegorically portrayed as the archetypal image of a peaceful rural community, an unspecified traditional lottery is held each year on June 27. The residents who gathered for the lottery are introduced; some individual names are mentioned. Further preparations are described, giving the reader some details about the lottery and its history. At the beginning of the lottery, members of each village family are called to draw lots according to well-defined rules. After the drawing of the lots, they are checked more closely. When it turns out that Bill Hutchinson has drawn a special lottery, his wife Tessie reacts with panicked behavior. There will be a new drawing, in which all members of the Hutchinson families will be drawn once again. This time, there's a black spot on the lot of Tessie Hutchinson. Then, at the end of the story, she is stoned to death by all the inhabitants of the village settlement. They believe that the well-being of their community depends on the described ritual, which has existed as a tradition since the founding of the village, although its origin and the exact background have been obscured in the course of history.
Due to the strict chronological structure of the plot with numerous retarding elements, the reader, despite occasional indications of an unexpected outcome of the lottery, only at the end of the story becomes shockingly aware of what fate awaits the drawn person.

story_text_a:
On a trip to an amusement park in Northern Ireland, British soldier Jody is seduced by the attractive Jewish woman and lured into a trap by the Irish Republican Army. The terrorist group threatens to kill him in order to free a comrade arrested by the police. The rather mild-mannered co-conspirator Fergus, who is assigned by Maguire, the head of the group, to guard the kidnapped Jody, quickly befriends the Afro-European, and Jody shows him a stolen photo of himself and his beautiful girlfriend, Dil. When the British government refuses to comply with the IRA's demands, Fergus is ordered to execute Jody. Fergus is struggling with himself. When he hesitates to execute Jody's death sentence, Jody can escape.
Escaping Fergus through the woods, Jody is run over by a passing British troop transport. The British army will be alerted to the terrorists, they will fly up, and their quarters will be shot down. Fergus manages to escape with his skin intact, and travels to London with a new identity, where he finds work on construction. "Jimmy", as he now calls himself, tracks down Jody's girlfriend, to whom he wants to convey the dead man's last message. However, the seductive and sensual Dil so captivates Fergus that he withholds the dead man's message. She takes him to her apartment, which is decorated with an installation of Jody's portraits and memorabilia of her lover. Fergus only discovers when he tries to sleep with her that she has a penis - a fact she thought he knew, since he approached her in a gay bar.
He beats her, runs away in shock. He tries to stay away from Dil, but is still drawn to her. Ferguson's situation becomes complicated when the two supposedly dead combatants Jude and Maguire show up at his place. The two of them are plotting an assassination attempt on a London judge, and they need Fergus to carry it out. Fergus initially refuses, but is forced to do so by the ruthless Jewess, who threatens to harm Dil otherwise.
In vain, Dil tries to get out of Fergus what he's hiding from her, what he's afraid of.
On the day of the planned assassination, Fergus is tied to the bed by Dil and held captive. She's figured out Fergus' connection to Jody by now, but she still loves the melancholy Irishman.
When Fergus doesn't show up as scheduled, Maguire attempts to shoot the judge himself, but is shot by the judge's bodyguards. A Jew escapes from a crime scene and seeks revenge. When she tries to make Dil pay for the failed assignment, she shoots her. Fergus forces Dil to flee, covers her tracks at the crime scene, turns himself in to the police as Jude's alleged killer to keep her out of jail. Sentenced to a lengthy prison term, he regularly receives visits from Dil, who waits outside for his release.
story_text_b: Three young men (Jacques, Pierre and Michel) share an apartment in Paris having many girlfriends and parties; during the film, they have signed a contract never to allow a girl to spend more than one night at their place. During one party, a friend of Jacques' tells him he has a compromising package (which turned out to be heroin) to deliver, and asks Jacques if he can leave it discreetly at their place. Jacques agrees and, as he works as a steward, flies away for a one-month trip in Japan telling Pierre and Michel about the package. One of Jacques' former girlfriends drops a baby before their door, making Pierre and Michel believe it is the package they are waiting for. Their lives change completely. The movie follows the bachelors as they deal with angry gangsters, suspicious cops, and the overwhelming responsibility of fatherhood.

story_text_a: Terry Brogan just got fired from the football team run by the super-rich Mrs. Wyler. Jake Wise, an old acquaintance, assigned him to track down Jessie, Mrs. Wyler's daughter, who went missing after a heated argument. He meets the young heiress in Mexico and it's the beginning of a great love. The team's coach, on Wise's orders, sets out to find them and surprises them in their hiding place.
story_text_b: Kim is a young orphan, wandering the streets of Lahore. One day he meets a lama and agrees to follow him on an initiatory quest. When the British authorities discovered his origin, he was placed in an English school. His taste for freedom is ill-suited to the discipline expected of an officer's son of Her Gracious Majesty. His knowledge of the Indians and their customs as well as his ability to impersonate an Indian would make him a spy for the British, who were trying to prevent a revolution in India.

story_text_a:
The film opens with the quote "The intoxication of combat often becomes a powerful and deadly addiction. The rush of battle is a potent and often lethal addiction, for war is a drug. by Chris Hedges, war correspondent and journalist for the New York Times.
Iraq 2004, early in the occupation of Iraq: A U.S. Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team loses its superior, Sergeant Thompson, while clearing a cloaked bomb. The battle-hardened and rugged Sergeant James is to replace him. James, who previously served in Afghanistan, is completely different from his caring predecessor, and so tensions soon arise in the team during the first deployments. Sergeant James is proving to be a reckless daredevil who doesn't care much for communicating with his team. Sergeant Sanborn and Specialist Eldridge soon wonder if, with James as team leader, they'll survive the few days until their return home.
While defusing bombs, they're even considering assassinating their superior officer. Sanborn hesitates, James does not notice anything. Shortly thereafter, the team gets into a firefight with insurgents. Under adverse conditions, the men successfully defend themselves. This experience seems to completely change the mood of the team. Back at their base, they get drunk together and James reveals some of his life to his men. He is the father of a son and still lives with the child's mother, but he feels emotionally separated from her. Also, his comrades discover a box under his bed containing parts of the bombs that James had previously disarmed. The box also contains his wedding ring, as the box contains everything that almost killed him.
On one mission, the team breaks into an abandoned terrorist hideout. There they find the embalmed body of a boy James thinks he knows. In his opinion, it is a DVD dealer, nicknamed "Beckham", with whom James had become friends. The boy was implanted with explosives. The normal course of action would be to destroy the bomb with an explosive charge, but James decides to disarm the bomb. He thus enables the boy to have a dignified burial. On the mission, the team is accompanied by a psychologist with the rank of lieutenant colonel, who wants to prove to Eldridge that he can stand by his man like any soldier in the field. He is trying to drive out some Arabs who are transporting stones there in a donkey cart. He addresses the Arabs in a friendly manner, shakes their hands, answers questions about his origin, and compliments the men from the danger zone with the utmost politeness. The group is about to leave. Except for the lieutenant colonel, everyone's already in the Humvee. As he waves to the Arabs, he is torn to pieces by a booby trap, presumably placed there by the Arabs. Eldridge only finds his helmet.
James wants to solve the boy's death and tries to blackmail information from a man who knew the boy. But this one leads him astray and disappears. That same night, the team is called into action. The men are to investigate the cause of the explosion of a tanker truck. Against regulations, James is attempting on his own to apprehend the bombers he suspects to be in the vicinity. A firefight ensues, and Eldridge is abducted by the terrorists. In the subsequent liberation of Eldridge, by James and Sanborn, he is wounded in the thigh. He's leaving Iraq to be treated at home.
For the final days and one last mission, the team now has to fight two by two: an Iraqi man was chained to a bomb. The men are unable to defuse them in time, and they have to leave the man behind. On the way back, Sanborn collapses in the car. He explains that he is no longer able to cope with the pressure of his assignment. Back home, he'll try to start a family, Sanborn said. He wants to know from James how he's coping with this burden, especially since bomb-sharpening, in Sanborn's opinion, is a constant gamble on life and death.
After they return home, James is seen trying to carry out his daily duties. It seems he can't blend in with the civilian world. In his mind, he's still in Iraq. One night, he explains to his two-year-old son that there is only one thing left for him "that he really loves". In the next scene, you see James back in Iraq; he's committed for another year.
story_text_b:
During the Iraq War, the American demining team, commanded by Sergeant James, was tasked with disarming the many improvised explosive devices in the area; this at the risk of their lives, but also those of the American soldiers responsible for their protection and Iraqi civilians. Sergeant First Class Will James, a cynical and disillusioned man, seems to be taking reckless risks. Initially poorly perceived by his teammates, these, in the long run, appreciate his professionalism in combat and his human qualities. However, tensions remain.
# Detailed synopsis
During the second year of the Iraq War, a U.S. Army Explosives and Munitions Deactivation Team with Bravo Company identifies and attempts to destroy an improvised explosive device with a robot, but the wagon carrying the detonation charge breaks. The team leader, Staff Sergeant Matthew Thompson, places the charge by hand, but is killed when a man with a cell phone detonates the charge. Fellow specialist Owen Eldridge feels guilty for not killing the man on the phone.
Sergeant First Class William James is replacing Staff Sergeant Thompson. He often disagrees with Sergeant J.T. Sanborn because he prefers to disarm devices by hand and does not communicate his plans. He blocks Sanborn's view with smoke grenades as he approaches a booby-trapped device and defuses it only moments before a man attempts to blow it up with a 9-volt battery. In another incident, James insists on disarming a complex car bomb despite Sanborn's protests that it takes too long; James responds by removing his helmet and "turning" Sanborn around. He is so disturbed by his conduct that he openly suggests Owen strike James while they detonate unused ammunition outside the base.
On their way back to their base, they encounter five armed men in Arab suits in an SUV with a flat tire. After a tense encounter, James learns that they are friendly British PMCs. While repairing the tire, they're under sniper fire. Three British are killed before James and Sanborn regain control, killing three insurgents. Eldridge kills the fourth one who tries to flank their position.
During a raid on a warehouse, James discovers a "body bomb" that he believes is Beckham, an Iraqi boy who sells DVDs and plays football outside the base. During the evacuation, Lt. Col. John Cambridge, the camp psychiatrist and Eldridge's advisor, was killed in an explosion; Eldridge was further traumatized. James sneaks off the base with Beckham's apparent associate at gunpoint, telling him to take him to Beckham's. He's left at the home of an independent Iraqi teacher and James runs away.
Called in to the detonation of an oil tanker, James decides to hunt down the insurgents responsible nearby. Sanborn protests, but when James starts a chase, he and Eldridge follow. After their separation, the insurgents captured Eldridge. James and Sanborn save him, James accidentally hits Eldridge. The next morning, James is approached by Beckham, alive and well, whom James ignores and passes by in silence. Before being airlifted for surgery, Eldridge angrily blames James for his injury.
The day before their deployment ends, they are called upon to disarm a suicide bomb attached to a man against his will. James can't cut the locks before the deadline expires and they're forced to abandon the man. Sanborn is helpless and tells James he has to leave Iraq and have a son.
After Bravo Company's rotation ends, James returns to his ex-wife Connie and their infant son. However, he is bored with the routine civilian life at home. James confesses to his son that there's only one thing he loves. He begins another one-year tour of duty with Delta Company.

story_text_a:
Terry Randall, die aus wohlhabendem Hause stammt und sich gegen den Willen ihres Vaters für die Schauspielerei entschieden hat, zieht in ein New Yorker Wohnheim für Theaterleute. Mit ihrer hochnäsigen Art eckt sie bei den anderen Nachwuchsschauspielerinnen schnell an. Besonders ihre neue Zimmergenossin, die Tänzerin Jean Maitland, kann Terry von Anfang an nicht ausstehen. Die Einzige, die zu Terry hält, ist die alternde Schauspielerin Catherine Luther, die sich als ihre Mentorin versteht. Als der einflussreiche Theaterproduzent Anthony Powell Jean tanzen sieht, verlässt er Linda, seine Geliebte. Anschließend verschafft er Jean ein Engagement in einem Nachtclub und beginnt mit ihr auszugehen. Zwar hatte Jean zunächst keine romantischen Absichten Powell gegenüber, doch findet sie allmählich Gefallen an ihm.
Die allseits beliebte Kay Hamilton, die ein Jahr zuvor auf der Bühne sehr erfolgreich war und hervorragende Kritiken bekommen hat, hat seither kein neues Angebot erhalten und daher auch kein Geld verdienen können. Sie hofft darauf, in Powells neuestem Bühnenstück die Hauptrolle zu ergattern. Als sie endlich vor Powell vorsprechen darf, sagt dieser den Termin in letzter Minute ab. Aufgrund ihrer Enttäuschung und als Folge von Unterernährung bricht Kay in der Eingangshalle zusammen. Als sich Terry deswegen mit Powell anlegt und ihm Vorwürfe macht, beginnen ihre Kolleginnen sie in einem neuen Licht zu sehen.
Terrys Vater will indes Powells neues Stück finanzieren – jedoch nur unter der Bedingung, dass seine Tochter die Hauptrolle erhält. Powell lädt Terry daraufhin in sein Penthouse ein, um ihr sein Angebot zu unterbreiten. Als Jean dort plötzlich ebenfalls eintrifft, nutzt Terry die Gelegenheit, um Jean die Augen über den stets untreuen Powell zu öffnen. Terry gibt vor, Powell versuche sie zu verführen. Ihr Plan funktioniert zwar, führt jedoch auch zu neuen Spannungen im Wohnheim. Jean will erneut nichts mehr mit ihr zu tun haben, und Kay ist am Boden zerstört, als sie erfährt, dass Terry die Hauptrolle erhalten hat.
Terry ist jedoch während der Proben so schlecht, dass Powell seine Vereinbarung mit ihrem Vater rückgängig machen will. Kurz vor der Premiere begeht Kay aus Verzweiflung Selbstmord. Terry ist wie alle anderen bestürzt über die Nachricht. Sie will keinesfalls auftreten. Catherine meint jedoch, dass die Show in Gedenken an Kay weitergehen müsse. Terry tritt schließlich doch auf und liefert eine emotionale und tief bewegende Vorstellung. Das Stück wird ein Hit und Terry und Jean beschließen, ihr Kriegsbeil zu begraben.
story_text_b: This is New York, 1937. In a girls' boarding school, young actresses find their destinies intertwined. A new play is staged and one of the girls, Jean, becomes the businessman's mistress. Another, Terry Randall, is an ambitious and self-righteous girl but a terrible actress: detested by her peers because of her meticulous diction and her large wardrobe, she wants to pursue her career at all costs. Kaye, the most gifted actress of all, manages to get the main part but Terry's wealthy father, financing the staging of the new play without the knowledge of the group, makes sure that his daughter gets the part even though he knows that she has no talent. Kaye, seeing the part blown out, suffers from it to the point of committing suicide on the very night of the show, but before doing so he gives Terry advice on how to hold the calles in his arms in the opening scene, as if they were a child. Terry takes her place and in the debut performance, moved by her friend's death, she finally plays with all the emotion she can express. In her final public speech, behind closed doors, she puts aside her arrogance and gives vent to her true feelings by becoming the most popular girl in the group.

story_text_a:
Au début des années 1990, durant un été très chaud, un embouteillage causé par un chantier de travaux publics paralyse de bon matin une portion d'autoroute de Los Angeles. Du fait de la chaleur, l'un des conducteurs bloqués, un homme ayant l'apparence d'un employé de bureau tout droit sorti de la fin des années 1950, craque soudainement et abandonne son véhicule. Laissant sa voiture, dont la plaque d'immatriculation personnalisée indique « D-FENS » au beau milieu de l’embouteillage, l'homme part à pied à la recherche d’une cabine téléphonique.
Alors qu'il demande à un vendeur de supérette de la petite monnaie afin de téléphoner à une cabine publique, l'homme se heurte au refus de l'épicier, un individu d'origine coréenne. Pour avoir sa monnaie, le vendeur l'oblige à acheter une canette de soda à un prix que l'homme juge prohibitif, car elle l'empêcherait de passer son coup de fil. Après en avoir débattu avec le commerçant, l’homme, ulcéré par le comportement du vendeur, l'accuse d'être un voleur qui a profité des largesses de son pays d'adoption. Puis, s'emparant de la batte de baseball brandie par l'épicier apeuré, il se met en colère et saccage le petit commerce quand le commerçant lui annonce le prix des diverses denrées de son établissement. Terrifié par le coup de sang de l'homme, l'épicier accepte finalement de lui vendre la canette de soda au prix qu'il juge juste. L'homme quitte peu après les lieux, emportant la batte du commerçant.
Après le départ du forcené, l'épicier se rend au commissariat pour porter plainte. Il y est accueilli par le détective du LAPD Martin Prendergast, un enquêteur de la criminelle proche de la retraite, qui décide de consacrer son dernier jour de travail à retrouver l'homme avant qu'il n'arrive un malheur. Pendant ce temps, l'homme téléphone à son ex-femme, Beth, mais celle-ci refuse de le laisser voir leur petite fille Adele, dont c'est l'anniversaire ce jour-là. Apparemment perturbé psychologiquement par cette séparation, l'homme lui dit qu'il « revient à la maison », Beth lui rétorquant qu'elle n’hésitera pas à appeler la police.
Alors qu'il se repose sur un terrain vague, ayant mal aux pieds à cause de ses chaussures de ville, l'homme est accosté par deux membres d'un gang de chicanos qui tentent de lui extorquer son attaché-case en le menaçant d'un couteau ; utilisant la batte de baseball prise à l'épicier, l'homme se défend et parvient à mettre en fuite les voyous, récupérant au passage l'une de leurs armes. Plus tard, les membres du gang le recherchent en voiture ; lorsqu'ils le retrouvent, les voyous lui tirent dessus mais manquent leur cible et sont peu après victimes d'un accident de la route qui tue plusieurs d'entre eux. L'homme en profite et subtilise dans la voiture accidentée un sac de sport rempli d'armes à feu, puis tire dans la jambe du gangster survivant pour lui donner une leçon. Peu après, l'homme abandonne son attaché-case, le donnant à un mendiant dans un parc qui insistait pour avoir quelque chose. La mallette est vide, mis à part le déjeuner frugal de l'homme que le mendiant, dégoûté, jette à terre.
L'homme se rend ensuite dans un fast-food, le Whammy Burger, où il exige qu'on lui serve un petit déjeuner alors que l'horaire où sont servis ce type de repas vient juste de se terminer. Après avoir eu un différend à ce sujet avec Rick, le responsable de l'établissement, l'homme sort un pistolet-mitrailleur de son sac et le brandit pour appuyer son point de vue selon lequel « le client a toujours raison ». Mais, changeant finalement d'avis, l'homme opte pour un déjeuner et, alors qu'il essaie d'apaiser la tension en parlant aux autres clients du restaurant (pétrifiés de peur autour de lui), il tire par inadvertance une rafale de son arme au plafond, la détente du pistolet-mitrailleur s'avérant très sensible. Après avoir reçu son repas, l'homme en critique l'aspect, mettant en parallèle la représentation publicitaire aguicheuse de son burger qu'il voit affiché sur les murs du restaurant avec le résultat réel qu'il a devant lui.
Poursuivant sa route, l'homme achète à un marchand ambulant un cadeau d'anniversaire pour sa fille, puis tente à plusieurs reprises d'appeler son ex-femme au téléphone. À un moment, une autre personne tente d'utiliser la cabine téléphonique où il se trouve, mais l'homme, excédé, détruit celle-ci avec son pistolet-mitrailleur. Dans le même temps Beth, son ex-femme, contacte la police en les informant de l'identité de l'homme (William Foster, un ancien salarié de l'industrie de la Défense, depuis peu au chômage) ainsi que des soucis psychologiques présents chez lui. Cependant, les policiers ne lui sont pas d'une grande aide.
Foster arrive ensuite dans un magasin de surplus militaire afin de s'acheter une paire de chaussures de marche. Il y fait la connaissance du propriétaire, Nick, un néo-nazi par ailleurs homophobe revendiqué. Nick, qui écoute illégalement la fréquence radio de la police, se rend compte que Foster est recherché par les autorités et le prend pour un milicien. Lorsqu’une inspectrice du LAPD arrive dans la boutique pour demander s'il a vu Foster, Nick protège celui-ci en mentant à la policière. Puis, il emmène son nouvel ami dans son arrière-boutique, et lui montre des souvenirs de la Première et Seconde Guerre mondiale (notamment une boîte de Zyklon B), ainsi qu'un lance-roquette moderne compact. Mais, étant en désaccord avec ses idéaux xénophobes, Foster le rejette. Furieux, Nick le met en joue avec son pistolet puis fouille son sac, détruisant le cadeau que Foster avait acheté pour sa fille en parlant d'un « truc de pédés ». Il tente ensuite de le menotter pour le livrer à la police et fantasme sexuellement sur lui, imaginant que Foster va se faire violer par des Noirs en prison. Mais Foster se rebelle et, après s'être battu contre Nick, finit par lui planter dans l'épaule le couteau subtilisé aux chicanos, et l'achève en lui tirant dessus avec son arme. Ce faisant, la folie de Foster atteint le point de non-retour. Il quitte le magasin après avoir changé de tenue pour arborer un treillis de G.I, emportant le lance-roquette.
En chemin, Foster tombe sur le site de travaux publics qui avait causé l'embouteillage au début du film. Avisant l'un des employés du chantier, il lui affirme que son patron facture des travaux injustifiés pour conserver son budget. Il s'énerve, sort le lance-roquette et (après avoir reçu des conseils de la part d'un garçon qui était sur les lieux) tire par accident dans une canalisation en travaux, la faisant exploser.
Son parcours le mène ensuite sur un terrain de golf privé, où un joueur âgé le réprimande de son intrusion puis le vise avec sa balle de golf. Foster réplique en sortant un fusil à pompe de son sac, puis tire sur la voiturette de golf des joueurs (dont les freins lâchent et qui dévale la pente vers un étang), critiquant dans le même temps l'utilisation faite de ce lieu alors qu'il devrait être, selon lui, plus utile en tant que parc public qu'un golf privé. Le joueur âgé est alors victime d'une crise cardiaque ; pendant que son collègue va chercher du secours, le malheureux réclame ses pilules qui se trouvent dans la voiturette. Mais Foster, cyniquement, lui répond que s'il l'avait laissé traverser tranquillement « son » golf, il ne serait pas en train de mourir avec un chapeau ridicule sur la tête, puis passe son chemin.
Pendant ce temps, le détective Prendergast apprend petit à petit que Foster — dont le nom n'est prononcé qu'une seule fois dans tout le film — a perdu son emploi dans le secteur de la Défense car il n'est plus « économiquement viable », que son mariage s'est désintégré et qu'il n'a pas le droit de voir sa fille, ayant harcelé son ex-femme Beth. Prendergast, ayant lui-même perdu une fille en bas âge, craint que ce déséquilibré ne tue sa famille dans un moment de folie.
Continuant sa route, Foster se rapproche du domicile de son ex-femme en passant par la luxueuse propriété d'un chirurgien esthétique. Il surprend le gardien et sa famille se baignant dans la piscine, les prend pour les propriétaires et les rudoie car il s'est blessé à la main avec le grillage de la clôture. Entendant une sirène de police, Foster prend la main de la fillette du gardien et conduit la famille un peu plus loin, pour les mettre à l'abri (ces derniers croyant à tort qu'il les a pris en otages). L'alerte passée, Foster se morfond sur son sort, évoquant avec amertume la séparation d'avec son ex-femme, l'amour qu'il porte pour sa fille et son désir de « revenir à la maison », puis quitte les lieux.
Lorsqu'il arrive enfin aux alentours de la maison de son ex-femme, située sur Venice Beach, Foster rate de peu Beth quand celle-ci l'aperçoit au loin et prend la fuite avec sa fille, les deux partant se réfugier vers la jetée où ils avaient, autrefois, tous les trois l'habitude d'aller se promener. Dans la maison vide, Foster regarde une ancienne cassette vidéo des jours heureux (sur laquelle ses troubles mentaux, qui lui causent des accès de rage, apparaissent déjà), et comprend soudainement que Beth est partie sur la jetée.
Le détective Prendergast, de son côté, laisse tomber son pot de départ au commissariat (qui ne finit pas comme prévu) et arrive sur les lieux. Il y retrouve Foster, qui a alors rejoint son ex-femme et sa fille sur la jetée, et comprend que celui-ci est armé. Après avoir l'avoir désarmé et fait évacuer les deux femmes, Prendergast tente de raisonner Foster en attendant l'arrivée des renforts. Le mettant en joue avec son arme, il lui affirme qu'il n'est qu’une victime de la récession parmi tant d'autres, et que cela ne lui donne pas le droit de se venger sur tout le monde. Foster réplique en annonçant au policier qu'il a sur lui un autre pistolet, et lui propose de faire un duel. Quelques instants plus tard, Foster dégaine un pistolet à eau ; Prendergast, croyant avoir affaire à une arme réelle, tire sur Foster et le tue, son corps chutant à la renverse dans la mer.
Après ce drame, Beth organise malgré tout la fête d'anniversaire de sa fille, celle-ci n'ayant pas vu les derniers instants de son père. Sur les conseils de Prendergast, Beth accepte d'en parler à sa fille le lendemain. Avant de partir, le policier discute également avec la fillette sur le perron de la maison de Beth, lui révélant à cette occasion qu'il va renoncer à prendre sa retraite.
story_text_b:
William Foster is recently divorced, has a restraining order from his ex-wife Beth, and has been fired from his job. When the air conditioning in his car stops working, he abandons it in the middle of a traffic jam and starts to walk, causing a commotion among the stranded motorists behind him. A motorcycle patrolman and Sergeant Prendergast help to place the car on the ledge so as not to obstruct the already congested traffic.
At a convenience store, the Korean owner refuses to give him change for a phone call and Foster complains about the high prices. During the argument, the owner pulls out a baseball bat. Foster wrestles it away and uses it to destroy his merchandise. Then he pays for a Coke, takes the change so he can make the call, and he leaves. Shortly after, he is approached by two gang members, who begin to follow him after leaving the self-service, provoke him, insult him and demand his briefcase. A gang member pulls out a knife and Foster fights them using the baseball bat. The fight ends with Foster getting the knife.
Meanwhile, Sergeant Prendergast, on his last day before retiring, takes a statement from the owner of the drive-through after his fight with Foster.
Foster's calling Beth from a pay phone. Despite the restraining order, he insists on going home to pick up his daughter, Adele, to celebrate her birthday. The gangsters, now in a car and with more men, find Foster. They attempt to assassinate him in revenge for the botched robbery minutes earlier by firing machine guns from the car, but only hit nearby witnesses before crashing into another vehicle and injuring themselves. Foster approaches the car, shoots the gang member in the leg who threatened him with the knife and who is trapped in the vehicle and takes the bag full of weapons with which they tried to kill him. Meanwhile, Beth calls the police frightened by Foster's calls and his insistence on going to Adele's birthday party, but the officers don't believe Foster is dangerous.
Foster walks through a park full of homeless people, one of them asking for a handout before complaining that Foster has two bags while he has nothing. Foster relents and gives the homeless man his briefcase, which contains only Foster's lunch. The homeless man protests furiously while Foster continues on his way with only the bag of guns.
Angela, the girlfriend of one of the accidented gang members, is questioned by the police as she witnessed the car assault. Angela describes Foster and Prendergast connects the self-service incident to the shooting, though his colleagues dismiss and ignore it.
Meanwhile, at a fast-food joint, Foster tries to order breakfast, but they've already changed the lunch menu seven minutes early. After an argument with the manager, who refuses to give him breakfast, Foster pulls out a machine gun and accidentally shoots the false ceiling. After trying to reassure the terrified employees and customers that he won't hurt anyone, Foster relents and orders lunch instead of breakfast, but then complains when the hamburger he is handed doesn't look anything like the one shown in the menu photo. He leaves the premises and tries to call Beth from a pay phone. After being insulted by an impatient man waiting for his turn to call, he destroys the phone booth with the same machine gun, rendering the phone useless, and leaves.
Prendergast and his partner, Torres, start investigating and find the traffic jam where Foster left his car. Prendergast sees the license plate of the car he saw this morning and it says "D-FENS".
Foster walks past a bank, where an African-American man protests that they have refused to grant him the loan, as according to the bank "it is not economically viable". As the police take him away, he exchanges a look with Foster and says, "Don't forget me". Whatever Foster nods, as if he agrees with the man.
Then Foster walks into a military supply store. The owner, a white supremacist, insults two gay customers and, when Torres arrives and asks him about Foster, he denies having seen him, while Foster is hidden in the dressing room. When she leaves, the owner congratulates Foster on the fast food incident, believing that all the employees were black, and offers Foster a rocket launcher. When Foster expresses his displeasure at the owner's racism, the owner subdues him, pulls out a gun, and attempts to handcuff him to the police, but Foster stabs him with the knife he confiscated from the gang members and shoots him to death with his own gun. Foster decides to change his clothes so as not to be recognized and dresses as a soldier with boots, as he had a hole in one of his shoes, and leaves with the rocket launcher and a new bag of weapons. He calls Beth again and tells her he's "coming home". Alarmed by his rambunctious and threatening speech, Beth again calls the police, who arrive and stay for a while.
Foster runs into some repairmen and accuses them of making unnecessary construction to justify his budget. He pulls out the rocket launcher, but he doesn't know how to use it. A child, who thinks they're filming a movie, teaches him how to operate the rocket launcher. While they're talking, Foster accidentally fires the rocket launcher at a lighthouse destroying the construction site.
Afterwards, Foster walks into a private golf club and walks across the field. A golfer yells at Foster for crossing and gives him a shot that Foster manages to dodge by throwing himself on the grass. Foster becomes enraged and pulls out a shotgun; he complains about the selfishness of the golfer and those accompanying him, saying that "they should have children playing" there. He shoots a golf cart containing the golfer's pills and the golfer suffers a heart attack. Fleeing the incident he arrives at an extravagant and luxurious house, where an employee of the owner holds a barbecue with his family. Foster complains about how he cut his hand with the barbed wire to get out of the golf course. He accidentally restrains the family by hearing voices and sirens but ends up letting them go.
Foster calls Beth again and mentions how he has changed her favorite ice cream shop, which is near the house. She hangs up the phone realizing she's out and manages to run off with Adele. Shortly after Foster arrives at the empty house and while watching old home videos on television with his daughter and ex-wife, Prendergast and Torres arrive. Foster in his escape shoots and wounds Torres and runs to the Venice Pier which is Beth's favorite place, while an unarmed Prendergast grabs Torres' gun and chases after him. At the end of the pier, Foster finds Beth and Adele. Adele is happy to see him and Foster puts his gun on the floor and hugs her, despite Beth's fear. Prendergast arrives and intervenes. Beth kicks the gun away from the distracted Foster, picks it up and throws it into the sea while Prendergast pulls out his revolver. Although he sympathizes with Foster's complaints about being trampled by society, Prendergast does not accept them as an excuse for the destruction and death he has caused and demands that he surrender. Undeterred by acknowledging that he is the "bad guy" in this story, Foster tells Prendergast that he has a concealed revolver. Taking it out, he has Prendergast shoot him before he realizes the weapon was a water pistol and gets him wet. Foster dies and falls off the pier into the sea. After conversing with Beth and Adele, Prendergast decides not to retire as a police officer that day.

story_text_a:
Im Sinne der göttlichen Komödie, handelt der Roman von einer Flucht des Helden vor sich selbst. In dieser mit Menschen überfüllten Welt beginnt für seine Wahrnehmung ein Inferno, der Abstieg in die Hölle. Die Handlung gleicht einem Roadmovie, das als Psychogramm beginnend, sich von einem Krimi zu einem perversen Horrortrip entwickelt, bis das Geschehen zum völligen Zusammenbruch führt. Der Held entkommt, in dem er in einem Science-Fiction-Märchen erwacht. Mit seinem Selbstmord beamt er sich anschließend in eine Realität, in der er als scheinbar vollkommener Mensch, mit der geliebten Frau und dem ungeborenen Kind, gleichnishaft wieder aufersteht, was der Idee christlicher Trinität, als auch dem Wunsch nach dem Paradies auf Erden entsprechen könnte.
Die Hauptfigur, Jeremy Bremen, verliert im Lauf der Story seine Frau Gail. Nach ihrem Tod ist Bremen nicht mehr in der Lage, die fremden, eindringenden Gedanken der ihn umgebenden Menschen abzuwehren. Sein Gedankenschirm bricht ein. Er versinkt in tiefe Depression. Als Mathematiker und angesehener Dozent an der Uni von Philadelphia, hatten Gail und er, bevor die Krankheit ausbrach, eine sehr intensive Liebe, eine, für seine wissenschaftliche Arbeit sehr fruchtbare Symbiose gelebt. Durch einen gemeinsamen Besuch bei dem renommierten Neuroforscher Jacob Goldmann finden beide Wissenschaftler, in Form der jeweiligen Forschungsergebnisse des anderen, die Lösung des Problems. Durch das Zusammenfügen der Ergebnisse finden sie den alles erklärenden Puzzlestein. Bremen vertieft sich nach dieser Begegnung immer mehr in die Chaosmathematik, die scheinbar die letzten Fragen der Menschheit beantworten könnte. Kurz vor dem Tod seiner Frau entdeckt er damit die Gleichungen, die alles erklären könnten: Wie das Gehirn, das Denken hervorbringt, was Verstand ist, was Erinnerungen sind, was den Geist des Menschen hervorbringt und wie das alles mit dem Funktionieren des Universums zusammenhängen könnte. Er muss seine Arbeit unterbrechen, als Gail fast nicht mehr in der Lage ist, seine Gedanken zu lesen. Er bleibt bis zu ihrem Ende in Form seiner Geistberührung bei ihr. Als sie stirbt, stirbt ein Teil seiner selbst. Sein Gedankenschirm bricht ein. Er wird  von dem nun einschlagenden Neurobrabbeln, das von den unzähligen Gedanken der Menschen in sein Gehirn einströmt, in einen Zustand tiefen psychischen Leids geworfen. So brutal auf sich und seine nicht mehr zu steuernde Fähigkeit zurückgeworfen, lässt er alles hinter sich und begibt sich in das Martyrium quälender Seelenpein. Die niedrigsten Gedankenwellen ziehen ihn immer tiefer in das primitivste Dasein der Welt, das geprägt ist von fremden Gedanken, die aus dem ihn umgebenden Dasein in Gewalt, Leid, Krankheit, Lust, Misstrauen, Gier, Dummheit, Neid und ungeheurer Brutalität stammen. Seine Odyssee beginnt damit, dass er seine Farm anzündet und flieht.
Er landet in Miami in einer Fischerhütte. Dort wird er Zeuge, wie ein Gangster eine Leiche verschwinden lässt. Dieser entführt den unfreiwilligen Zeugen, um ihn von seinen Mafiakollegen umbringen zu lassen. Doch Bremen gelingt es, in Disney World unterzutauchen und als Goof verkleidet zu fliehen. Er steigt in einen Bus und landet nachts in Denver. Von einer der umherziehenden Jugendbanden ausgeraubt und krankenhausreif geschlagen, findet er sich in einer Klinik der Stadt wieder. Von seinen Gedanken getrieben und um den fremden Gedanken zu entkommen, flieht er noch in derselben Nacht. Er findet bei den Obdachlosen Zuflucht und verbringt eine scheinbar endlose Zeit als alkoholsüchtiger Penner unter den Brücken von Denver. In einem Anfall von angestauter Wut schlägt er einen Vergewaltiger eines Mädchens fast zu Tode. Wieder muss er fliehen. Soul Dad steckt ihn in einen geklauten 79er Pontiac. Aus Utah kommend, landet er in der Wüste. Miz Morgan lügt Deputy Depp an, dass Bremen ihr schon längst erwarteter, neuer Farmarbeiter sei und nimmt Bremen mit auf ihre Two-M Ranch. Auch hier verbringt er eine unbestimmte Zeit, bis das Geschehen zu einem völlig unerwarteten Horrortrip mutiert. Miz, die versucht, ihn auf grausame Weise zu töten, so wie sie es mit unzähligen anderen vor ihm schon getan hat, um ihn dann zu den anderen in ihr Tiefkühlhaus zu hängen, wird selbst zum Opfer. Dem Schauplatz dieses Horrors schwer verletzt entkommen, landet Jeremy auf der vorletzten Station seiner Höllenfahrt in Las Vegas. Zusammen mit seinem Gewinn von über 300.000 Dollar, wird Jeremy von drei Gangstern in einer Piper Cheyenne nach New Jersey entführt. Bremen soll dort von Don Leoni Leuten entsorgt werden. Hier schließt sich der Kreis: Vanni Fucci, der Ganove, hatte ihn auf dem Kontrollbildschirm eines der Casinos wiedererkannt. Nachdem Jeremy die Gedanken des Piloten studiert hat, kann er die Gangster in dem Flugzeug zu einer Schießerei provozieren. Er steuert die Maschine zu einer Bruchlandung.
Wieder ist er der Überlebende. Über seine Identität wissen die Behörden mittlerweile Bescheid, denn seine Fingerabdrücke sind unerklärlicherweise vorhanden. Im Krankenhaus wird er verhört. Wieder plant er akribisch seine nächste Flucht. Doch neben ihm liegt der schwer zugerichtete Robby. Er erinnert sich daran, wie gut es sich anfühlte, als er in Disneyland auf eine Gruppe schwerkranker Kinder traf. Hinter der Maskerade ihre Gedanken lesend, hatte er jedem Kind, den jeweils eigenen Trost gespendet. Ihn überkommt der Wunsch, dies auch mit Robby zu versuchen. In dessen unterentwickelten Geist eingedrungen, findet er sich in einer völlig idealisierten eigenen Welt wieder. Er und Gail sind plötzlich beide an diesem Ort, der offenbar ihrer beider Wahrnehmung entspricht. Er und Gails Geist sind Jeremys Theorie der Wahrscheinlichkeitswellenfronten zufolge, als Hologramme in Robbys Gehirn auferstanden, samt allen Vorstellungen und Erinnerungen ihrer gemeinsamen Realität. Gails Seele war offensichtlich in der Lage, sich im Moment des Todes in sein Gehirn zu retten. Um sich aus dem sterbenden Gehirn des Jungen zu befreien, muss Jeremy Gail wieder loslassen. Er erwacht aus einem Koma. Er hat offensichtlich fünf Tage mit Gail verbracht. 
Die Ärzte sind sprachlos. Man hatte ihn für tot erklärt. Als er wieder klar ist, setzt er seinen längst gefassten Plan durch und flieht zum letzten Mal. Hier endet der erzählerische Bogen: Wieder am Ufer des Ozeans angelangt, wo er die letzten Momente vor Gails Tod mit ihr durch Geistberührung teilte, erschießt sich Bremen.
story_text_b:
In the sense of divine comedy, the novel is about the hero's escape from himself. In this crowded world, his perception begins an inferno, a descent into hell. The plot resembles a road movie, which begins as a psychogram, evolves from a crime novel to a perverse horror trip, until the action leads to a complete breakdown. The hero escapes by waking up in a science fiction fairy tale. By his suicide he then beams himself into a reality where he is resurrected as a seemingly perfect man, with his beloved wife and unborn child, equally, which could correspond to the idea of the Christian Trinity, as well as the desire for paradise on earth.
The main character, Jeremy Bremen, loses his wife Gail in the course of the story. After her death, Bremen is no longer able to fend off the alien, intrusive thoughts of the people around him. His mind screen is breaking. He sinks into a deep depression. As a mathematician and distinguished lecturer at the University of Philadelphia, he and Gail, before the outbreak of the disease, had lived a very intense love, a symbiosis that was very fruitful for his scientific work. Through a joint visit to the renowned neuroscientist Jacob Goldmann, both scientists find the solution to the problem in the form of each other's research results. By piecing together the results, they find the puzzle stone that explains it all. After this encounter, Bremen delves deeper and deeper into the mathematics of chaos, which could seemingly answer the last questions of mankind. Shortly before his wife's death, he discovers the equations that could explain everything: how the brain produces thought, what mind is, what memories are, what produces the human mind, and how all of this could relate to the workings of the universe. He has to interrupt his work when Gail is almost unable to read his mind. He stays with her until the end in the form of his spirit touch. When she dies, a part of him dies. His mind screen is breaking. He is thrown into a state of profound psychological distress by the impactful neural babble that flows into his brain from the countless thoughts of people. So brutally thrown back on himself and his uncontrollable ability, he leaves everything behind and enters into the martyrdom of tormenting anguish. The lowest waves of thought pull him deeper and deeper into the most primitive existence of the world, marked by alien thoughts that come from the existence that surrounds him in violence, suffering, sickness, lust, mistrust, greed, stupidity, envy and monstrous brutality. His odyssey begins with him setting fire to his farm and fleeing.
He ends up in a fisherman's cabin in Miami. There, he witnesses a gangster dispose of a body. He kidnaps the unwilling witness to have him killed by his Mafia colleagues. However, Bremen manages to sneak into Disney World and escape disguised as a Goof. He gets on a bus and lands in Denver at night. Robbed and beaten to death by one of the youth gangs, he finds himself in a clinic in the city. Driven by his thoughts and to escape the alien thought, he flees that very night. He takes refuge with the homeless and spends a seemingly endless amount of time as an alcoholic bum under the bridges of Denver. In a fit of rage, he beats a girl's rapist almost to death. He'll have to run again. Soul Dad's putting him in a stolen '79 Pontiac. Coming from Utah, he ends up in the desert. Miz Morgan lies to Deputy Depp that Bremen is her long-awaited new farmhand and takes Bremen to her Two-M ranch. Here, too, he spends an indefinite amount of time until the action mutates into a completely unexpected horror trip. Miz, who tries to kill him in a cruel way, as she has done to countless others before him, to then hang him with the others in her freezer, becomes the victim herself. Escaping the scene of this horror with serious injuries, Jeremy lands on the penultimate leg of his journey to Las Vegas. Along with his winnings of over $300,000, Jeremy is kidnapped by three gangsters in a Piper Cheyenne and taken to New Jersey. Bremen is to be disposed of there by Don Leoni's people. Vanni Fucci, the gangster, had recognized him on the control screen of one of the casinos. After Jeremy has studied the pilot's thoughts, he can provoke the gangsters on the plane into a shootout. He's steering the plane into a crash landing.
He's the survivor again. His identity is now known to the authorities because his fingerprints are inexplicably present. He's being questioned at the hospital. Once again, he's meticulously planning his next escape. But next to him lies the severely wounded Robby. He remembers how good it felt to meet a group of seriously ill children at Disneyland. Behind the masquerade, reading their thoughts, he had given each child his own consolation. He gets the urge to do the same with Robby. Having penetrated his underdeveloped mind, he finds himself in a completely idealized world of his own. He and Gail are both suddenly in this place, which apparently corresponds to both of their perceptions. He and Gail's mind are, according to Jeremy's theory of probability wavefronts, when holograms resurrected in Robby's brain, along with all the notions and memories of their shared reality. Gail's soul was apparently able to escape into his brain at the moment of death. To free himself from the boy's dying brain, Jeremy must let go of Gail again. He's waking up from a coma. Apparently, he spent five days with Gail.
The doctors are speechless. He was declared dead. When he regains consciousness, he executes his long-planned plan and flees for the last time. Here ends the narrative arc: Once again on the shore of the ocean, where he shared the last moments before Gail's death with her by touch, Bremen shoots himself.

story_text_a:
The rats, led by Ben the Rat, kill their human master and master Willard after Willard tries to poison them, and go into hiding. Willard's mutilated body is discovered and a worried crowd gathers around his Los Angeles home. Police Detective Cliff Kirtland and his assistant Joe Greer are leading the investigation into Willard's brutal death. You'll find Willard's diary describing his friendship with Socrates, another rat, and Ben. It is considered better not to publish the diary at the moment, because in it Willard describes how he trained the rats to kill his superior Billy Hatfield who was treating him. Ben, who watches the men from a hiding place, has instructed his "family" to hide in the walls of the old mansion. While the police are waiting for health officials, officers Kelly and Reade are guarding the house. Reade goes to the basement where Willard has trained his animal helpers. With no more rats to be seen, Reade concludes that the animals are hiding behind the walls. When he rips out a panel, Ben instructs his buddies to kill the policeman. Kelly arrives too late to help his partner, and after examining the human remains, Kirtland hands Willard's diary to Billy Hatfield.
The next day Eve Garrison and her younger brother Danny, who is working on a very dangerous heart condition, spend the day together as usual. Since her father's death, Eve mostly stays home to take care of Danny while her mother Beth struggles to run the family business. In his own little world, a building near the house, Danny plays with his beloved puppets. As he begins his lunch, Ben approaches him through a hole. Danny's surprised, and he likes to share his sandwich with the smart rat. Danny, tired of being alone forever, is glad to have this animal companion with him, because obviously the rodent understands him when Danny speaks to him. The following night, Ben leads the rats to raid a food truck. The driver is so frightened that he collides with an oncoming car. The next day, a policeman informs the garrisons that the next morning the pest controllers requested by the health department will come to the neighborhood to set traps and spray rat poison. Danny tells his sister and mother about his new friend, the rat. Eve thinks her brother has too much imagination. But it does not rule out the possibility that it may be the very rat Willard mentioned in his diary, published in the newspaper in the meantime. It also mentions the rat's name, Ben.
Danny likes the name, and he's going to call his new four-legged friend Ben, too, not knowing it's actually Ben. That night, Danny writes a song about his friendship with Ben. Eve is very touched by the song parts. Shortly thereafter, Ben and his thousand-strong army of rats raid a supermarket. She eats all the rat meat there until she's discovered by a night watchman. Ben leads his followers into the sewers, where they make their new home in a huge, abandoned room. It can only be reached through an abandoned tunnel. During the day, Ben visits Danny's workshop again, where Danny performs a show for him with a rat puppet. Danny's relationship with Ben grows closer, and the boy, who suspects that Ben is the leader of the rat army, tells him that after the supermarket robbery, he should be more careful in the future so as not to fall into the clutches of the pest controllers. After Danny Bens (voiced by Michael Jackson) performs a song on his harmonica, Danny shows his furry friend the scar from his heart surgery. Danny watches the pest controllers set traps and poison around the Garrison house. To instruct Ben about the dangers of the traps, he demonstrates their effectiveness and makes it clear that they must be avoided. When a bigger and stronger boy starts to bully Danny, Ben and his disciples attack the boy and bite into his legs until he runs away. Danny's gonna tell Kirtland later that the kid got his injuries from falling into a rose bush.
When Danny mentions the name Ben, the grown-ups get all deaf. But he can make amends for his babbling by bringing out his rat puppet and declaring that it is his friend Ben of whom he has spoken. Back in the office, Kirtland and his subordinate Greer are talking to a city engineer. He claims that more than two hundred miles of sewers have been searched with no result and that it will take several days to complete the inspection of the entire sewer system. Kirtland insists on continuing the work. Meanwhile, Ben and his army break into a cheese shop next to a wellness center and scare off all the guests who want to lose a few pounds. The next day, Danny asks Ben to show him where he and his rat friends live. Danny follows Ben through the sewers and ends up in a room with thousands of rats. Although the animals' first instinct almost drives them to attack Danny, Ben's authority keeps them from attacking. Danny has trouble breathing and returns home. He hears on the radio that the police want to expand the rat extermination operation, and when Ben and some of his friends appear at the window, Danny hides them in his bed. As Eva glances in his room to see if her brother, who has a heart condition, is all right, she is shocked to find rats scattered all over his bed. Immediately, Mother Beth informs officers Kirtland and Greer.
When Danny is questioned, he stubbornly refuses to reveal Ben's whereabouts. Kirtland is now beginning to intensify the search for the rats in the sewers. When two workers in the sewers get too close to Ben's hiding place, he orders his followers to kill them. However, one of the two men may escape. Shortly thereafter, construction workers, police and firefighters, led by Kirtland and Greer, converge on the sewer entrance. They're trying to drown the rats with an elaborate plan. Danny rushes out into the open to find his friend Ben and warn him. In the process, he slips through a drain into the rat hole. Eve, look for Danny, follow him. Danny can track down Ben and ask him to flee immediately. But Ben makes it clear to Danny that he needs to get himself to safety. Then Eve finds her little brother. Both climb back into the daylight as Ben's army of rats fight the human attackers from underground. As the workers flee, Kirtland and Greer go downstairs to assess the situation. By joining forces, almost all rats will be exterminated. Danny returns sadly to his little hiding place when he hears a low squeak. He sees the wounded Ben who managed to escape the carnage. Overjoyed, Danny cares for his four-legged friend and promises to take good care of him in the future.
story_text_b:
The trio play medical school graduates whose only credentials are that they had the highest temperatures in their class. (They are hired as doctors at the Los Arms Hospital solely because they have been in their senior class for too many years.) The new graduates at the hospital are warned by the superintendent that the Stooges are "not overly bright," but it is promised that their identities will be concealed as long as they promise to devote their lives to "the glorious cause of duty and humanity", which prompts the three to step forward and thank him profusely for not being able to let their identities be known. The superintendent has told the Stooges to rush and answer the loudspeaker whenever their names are called. The short consists of a series of skits in which the Stooges go from one patient to the next, making mistakes ranging from drinking a patient's medicine to sewing their tools inside a man on the operating table.
Every time the Stooges leave the superintendent's office, Curly accidentally ends up breaking the glass door to his office. On their final entry a maintenance worker (having gotten tired of constantly replacing it) intentionally breaks the door for them and bows as they enter.
Each time the Stooges rush and answer the loudspeaker, a different scenario takes place:

story_text_a: L'histoire démarre aux Pays-Bas en octobre 1943. Un colonel néerlandais, Peter Deventer (interprété par Clark Gable), est fait prisonnier par les Allemands, puis libéré par des résistants hollandais. Les services secrets anglais lui demandent alors d'organiser cette résistance et de donner à cette dernière des missions précises. Il recrute et forme un agent de liaison, féminin, Carla Van Oven (Lana Turner) : ses sentiments pour celle-ci le font renoncer à l'envoyer en mission, mais elle insiste et part contacter le chef des résistants, Foulard (Victor Mature). Mais à partir du moment où les actions sont décidées par les services secrets anglais, les Néerlandais tombent systématiquement dans des embuscades, qui coûtent la vie à de nombreux hommes. Le colonel est renvoyé en mission pour démasquer le traître.
story_text_b: The story begins in the Netherlands in October 1943. A Dutch colonel, Peter Deventer (played by Clark Gable), is taken prisoner by the Germans, then freed by Dutch resistance fighters. The British secret services then asked him to organize this resistance and give it specific missions. He recruits and trains a female liaison officer, Carla Van Oven (Lana Turner): his feelings for her make him renounce sending her on a mission, but she insists and goes to contact the leader of the resistance, Foulard (Victor Mature). But from the moment the actions are decided by the English secret services, the Dutch systematically fall into ambushes, which cost many men their lives. The colonel is sent back on a mission to expose the traitor.

story_text_a:
In an unspecified future, a virus strikes girls between the ages of 15 and 17, causing them to experience an unusual euphoria, called "Near Death Happiness", then kills them and turns them into "Stacies", or zombies. To deal with the "Stacies", humanity has created special re-kill teams, called "Romeros", who kill the "Stacies" once and for all, tearing them apart.
An artist meets a girl at a critical age to be attacked by the virus, but still healthy. The two fall in love, despite the man being aware of the girl's imminent death, who begins to suffer the signs of the disease and is attacked by "Near Death Happiness".
Meanwhile, a doctor studies the virus, using some Stacies as guinea pigs, and discovers that it is due to Butterfly Twinkle Powder, a powder that accumulates on the skin of the girls, while television commercials are aired in which an electric saw is advertised to be used to chop up the Stacies, and a trio of girls of contagious age, dressed conspicuously, try to anticipate the re-killing teams, looking for the Stacies and getting paid to kill them.
story_text_b: Five years after obtaining the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, Jacques Monod surprises the scientific community with this controversial essay in which, when studying issues such as the origin of life or the evolution of species, he introduces such seemingly inappropriate concepts as azar and necessity; that is, he raises the metaphysical and spiritual implications of the great discoveries in the fields of molecular biology and genetics.[1][2]

story_text_a:
The story is set during the reign of King George III, in Bristol, England, where young Benjamin Blake (Roddy McDowall), son of the deceased Baronet of Breetholm is taken from his commoner grandfather, gunsmith Amos Kidder (Harry Davenport), and forced to serve his vengeful uncle, Sir Arthur Blake (George Sanders). Arthur inherited the title and land from his brother Godfrey, and fears that Ben may not have been born out of wedlock and might claim his inheritance. He compels the boy to become his ward and bonded servant, giving Arthur life-and-death power over the lad. Ben runs away to his grandfather, but rather than force the old man to live a life on the run, returns to Breetholm, vowing to endure whatever he must in order to one day prove himself a "true Blake" and recover his birthright.
Ben, now a young man (Tyrone Power), has fallen in love with Isabel (Frances Farmer), his cousin and Arthur's haughty and scheming daughter. Arthur discovers the relationship and thrashes Benjamin with his fists, then beats him unconscious and flogs him mercilessly when he retaliates. Ben confronts Arthur that night, but is threatened with jail for breaking into his room to assault him, a hanging offense. Ben flees arrest but his grandfather is imprisoned for helping Ben escape. Ben stows away on a ship bound for the South Seas, where he can make his fortune, prove his claim, and release his grandfather from prison. Ben is forced to join the ship's crew, but joins shipmate Caleb Green (John Carradine) in jumping ship at a Polynesian island. There he wins the trust of the native islanders, finds fortune (pearls), and takes a new love, a native girl he calls "Eve" (Gene Tierney). When a Dutch ship happens by, allowing them to fulfill their ambitions, Caleb discovers that the idyllic life in the islands is worth more than the pearls they have amassed, but Ben remains true to his vow and his imprisoned grandfather.
With their combined treasure, he returns to England under an assumed name to prove his birthright with the help of noted "man of influence," Bartholomew Pratt (Dudley Digges). Ben is betrayed after he goes to Breetholm to see Isabel, and is convicted by jury for the earlier offenses. Just as his death sentence is about to be pronounced, he is saved by Pratt, who proves that no crime was committed by showing that Ben's father and mother were married aboard a ship to India, and that "Sir Benjamin Blake" was in law the rightful baronet at the time. Ben discovers that it was Isabel who betrayed him and also repays the beating he received from Arthur. He emancipates the bonded tenants of Breetholm and divides the estate among them, deeding the manor house to his grandfather. Ben then returns to the Polynesian island to live out his life with Eve.
story_text_b:
The leaders of the secret organization "The Five Golden Dragons" meet in person for the first time in Hong Kong to share the profits from their thriving black market deals. But one of the gentlemen dies, prompting Mr. Porter, his lawyer, to travel to Hong Kong, where he, too, is murdered shortly after his arrival. A lead leads the local police to the American playboy and reporter Bob Mitchell, to whom Porter wanted to send a letter before his death. The letter contains the name of the organization in question, which will also soon learn of Mitchell. That's how they kill Margret, who's lying in Mitchell's bed instead. He and Margaret's sister Ingrid try to find out who is responsible for Margaret's death, narrowly escaping the organization's clutches. Meanwhile, the police are looking for Mitchell as a potential murderer of Margaret.
In the course of his investigation, Mitchell eventually comes across Peterson, a nightclub owner who works for the organization.
At the meeting of the chiefs, Peterson wants to use Mitchell as a replacement for the deceased dragon so he can cash in on it himself. Since the five leaders do not know each other, they have installed a sophisticated identification system: In the center of the conference table is a wooden pagoda with five small doors. Whoever's key matches his lock can open it and take off his mask. Anyone whose key doesn't match will be shot by the weapon strapped behind it when they open the door.
Mitchell allows himself to be persuaded, whereupon all five dragons assemble. One by one, they open their doors. The last dragon will be shot. Shortly thereafter, the police stormed the hall and arrested the four dragons. The dragon shot, however, is not Mitchell, but Peterson, from whom Mitchell escaped at the last moment, so that he himself had to slip into the role of the fifth dragon.

story_text_a:
Bob is a gambler who lives on his own in the Montmartre district of Paris, where he is well-liked by the demi-monde community. A former bank robber and convict, he has mostly kept out of trouble for the past 20 years, and is even friends with a police commissioner, Ledru, whose life he once saved. Ever the gentleman, Bob lets Anne, an attractive young woman who has just lost her job, stay in his apartment in order to keep her from the attentions of Marc, a pimp he hates. Bob declines Anne's advances, instead steering her to his young protégé Paolo, who soon sleeps with her.
Through Jean, an ex-con who is now a croupier at the casino in Deauville, Bob's friend Roger, a safecracker, learns that, by 5:00 in the morning on the day of a big horse race at the nearby track, the casino safe is expected to contain around 800 million French francs in cash. As Bob has had a run of bad luck, he plans to rob the safe, convincing a man named McKimmie to finance the preparations and recruiting a team to carry out the heist. Jean gets detailed floor plans of the casino and the specifications of the safe, and buys a bracelet for his wife, Suzanne, with some of the money he is paid for his services.
The smitten Paolo brags to Anne about the upcoming raid to try to impress her. Not taking him seriously, she lets this information slip to Marc just before the two have sex. Earlier, Marc had been arrested by Ledru for beating up one of his prostitutes, but Ledru had released him on the condition that he provide some information on a bigger crime; Marc's reaction makes Anne realize she may have made a mistake.
The next morning, Anne tells Bob what she did, and he and Roger search for Marc, but cannot find him. Marc tells Ledru that he has heard about a caper involving Bob, but needs a few more hours to obtain confirmation, so Ledru lets him go. When Bob tells Paolo about Marc and Anne, the young man finds Marc and shoots the man dead just as he is about to tell Ledru what he was able to find out. Meanwhile, Suzanne discovers where her husband got the money to buy the bracelet and decides to ask Bob for a larger share of the take. They drive to Paris, but are unable to find him or Roger. She then persuades Jean to back out of it and anonymously tips off Ledru.
Thinking that, with Marc dead, their plan is still a secret, Bob and his team head to Deauville. Ledru searches fruitlessly for Bob to convince him to abandon his plan. He reluctantly leads a convoy of armed police to the casino.
Bob enters the casino to check on things. The plan is that, unless he signals them otherwise, his team will burst in at 5:00 a.m. and rob the safe at gunpoint. He had promised Roger that he would not gamble until after the heist was over, but, after wandering around for a while, he cannot resist placing a bet.  He has an incredible run of good luck, first at roulette, then at chemin de fer, and loses track of the time. Just before 5:00, he finally looks at his watch. He orders the staff to cash his huge pile of chips and hurries out the door. The police arrive as Bob's team are walking toward the casino, and a shootout ensues; Paolo is shot. Bob comes upon the aftermath and holds Paolo as he dies. He and Roger are handcuffed and put into Ledru's car, and Bob's winnings are put in the trunk. Ledru says Bob will probably only spend three years in prison, but Roger says that, with a good lawyer, he will get acquitted. Bob quips that he may even sue for damages.
story_text_b: Robert Montagné, a hardcore gambler and frequent visitor to notorious gatherings, nicknamed "Bob the Gambler" precisely because of his great passion for gambling, finds himself broke, plans with acquaintances a robbery at the Deauville casino. Caught up in the game, however, he profoundly forgets the time and begins to win, blowing up the house and earning the money he was supposed to steal.

story_text_a:
Schlikov est employé chauffeur de taxi à Moscou, homme simple attaché aux valeurs du travail manuel, tandis que Liocha est un artiste saxophoniste qui « parle avec Dieu », vit en débauché et méprise le travail manuel. Deux mondes que tout oppose et qui, habituellement, s'ignorent.
Mais un jour, Liocha, accompagné de filles et de vodka, monte dans le taxi de Schlikov pour une nuit de débauche à travers la ville. Après plusieurs heures la fête tire à sa fin, et prétextant devoir aller chercher de quoi payer sa course chez lui, Liocha fausse compagnie à Schlikov, qui l'attend en vain jusqu'au matin. Énervé, Schlikov décide alors de retrouver celui qu'il voit comme un fêtard parasite pour récupérer son argent. Mais lorsqu'il y arrive, ce dernier s'avère ne pas pouvoir payer. Schlikov prend alors son saxophone en otage et force Liocha à travailler pour lui, tout autant pour être remboursé que pour l'« éduquer ».
Bien que tout les oppose, une certaine amitié semble finir par naître. Pourtant, lorsque Liocha rencontre le succès via Hal Singer, il laisse sans pitié tomber Schlikov, resté simple chauffeur de taxi.
story_text_b:
Schlikov is an employed taxi driver in Moscow, a simple man attached to the values of manual labor, while Liocha is a saxophone artist who  talks with God, lives in debauchery and despises manual labor. Two worlds that oppose each other and usually ignore each other.
But one day, Liocha, accompanied by girls and vodka, gets into Schlikov's taxi for a night of debauchery through the city. After several hours the party comes to an end, and under the pretext of having to go to get something to pay for his groceries at home, Liocha pretends company to Schlikov, who waits in vain until the morning. Annoyed, Schlikov then decides to track down what he sees as a parasitic partygoer to get his money back. But when he arrives, he finds himself unable to pay. Schlikov then takes his saxophone hostage and forces Liocha to work for him, as much to be reimbursed as to educate him.
Despite their differences, a certain kind of friendship seems to be born in the end. However, when Liocha finds success through Hal Singer, he ruthlessly abandons Schlikov, who remains a simple taxi driver.

story_text_a:
The Montellis, an Italian American family headed by Anthony Montelli and his wife, Dolores, move into 112 Ocean Avenue in Amityville, New York, with their children, Sonny, Patricia, Mark, and Jan.
An evil presence is shown to be lurking within the house, unknown to the family. Unusual and paranormal activities occur, such as unknown forces banging on the door at night when nobody is outside and an ugly demonic message being painted on the wall of Jan's room.
